clue.text: Unthinking, has joint as well as Charlie

parts.note: the knee is a joint of the leg
a charlie is British slang for a fool, as is a jerk

explanation.surface: A careless man who has a spliff and some cocaine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joint' and 'Charlie' suggest cannabis and cocaine; they are the knee and a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: A knee-jerk reaction is an automatic reflex made without thought, like the tap-on-the-knee reflex.

clue.text: It was a mistake to strike that Test failure

definitions.text: It was a mistake to strike that

indicators.note: a failed version of the word, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A batsman regretting a shot that cost the match in a cricket Test.
explanation.walkthrough: A Test is an international cricket match, which 'strike' plays on. Stet is the proof-reader's mark meaning 'let it stand'.
explanation.definitionFit: A proof-reader writes stet beside a deletion to cancel it, meaning the crossing-out was an error.

clue.text: Alternative fuel on Motorway's coming

parts.note: or introduces an alternative
gas is a fuel
M is the motorway prefix, as in the M1

explanation.surface: Green fuel is soon to be sold on the motorway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coming' looks like 'on its way'; it is sexual climax.
explanation.definitionFit: Coming is slang for reaching sexual climax, so the noun for that climax fits.

clue.text: Queasy, drunk Mexican-style, but not experiencing the usual runs

parts.note: feeling off means unwell

indicators.note: said in a mock Mexican accent, the slang word is turned into a different word

parts.note: pissed is British slang for drunk

explanation.surface: A tourist sick from tequila, but at least without the usual diarrhoea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The usual runs' suggests stomach trouble; it means marked ski runs. A piste is a groomed ski run.
explanation.definitionFit: Skiing off-piste means going away from the prepared, marked slopes onto untouched snow.

clue.text: Sporting an erection, having removed top and bottom of towelling garment

indicators.text: having removed top and bottom of
indicators.note: the first and last letters are taken away

parts.note: a bathrobe is made of towelling

explanation.surface: A man whose bathrobe has come off at both ends, revealing his arousal.
explanation.definitionFit: Athrob means throbbing, the pulsing state of something swollen, here a sexual sense.

clue.text: Think "sticky stuff" on date and enjoy satisfaction

parts.note: to feel something is to think or believe it
goo is any sticky substance

explanation.surface: Musing on bodily fluids during a date and having a satisfying time.
explanation.definitionFit: To feel good is to be contented and pleased, which is what satisfaction gives.

clue.text: Jumping sheep and the like

definitions.meaning: the surface reads it as leaping, but jumping is slang for having sex
beasts in general, so sex with animals

explanation.walkthrough: The picture is lambs bounding about a field; the cryptic sense is sex with animals.
explanation.definitionFit: Bestiality is sexual activity between a human and an animal, the crude reading of the clue.

clue.text: Kind-hearted whip? She could eat you for breakfast!

definitions.text: She could eat you for breakfast!

parts.note: big-hearted, generous; big means kind as in 'that's big of you'
the cat is the cat-o'-nine-tails

explanation.surface: A dominatrix with a heart of gold who could still devour you.
explanation.walkthrough: 'She could eat you for breakfast' suggests a formidable woman; it describes a lioness or tigress literally.
explanation.definitionFit: A lion, tiger or leopard is a predator large enough to eat a person; a lioness does the hunting.

clue.text: Catch whore with Hardy — a nice turn-up for the books

definitions.text: a nice turn-up for the books
definitions.note: a pleasing surprise in the accounts; noun phrase like the answer

parts.note: a catch is a haul landed in a net
a pro is slang for a prostitute
hardy and fit both mean robust and healthy

explanation.surface: A tabloid tale of a prostitute caught with a novelist, sold as a surprise for the publishers.
explanation.walkthrough: Hardy looks like Thomas Hardy the novelist, which suits 'books'; here it is just an adjective meaning fit.
explanation.definitionFit: Profit left after costs is a welcome surprise when the ledger is totted up, the books being a firm's accounts.

clue.text: Vulgar Italian reveals organ before perverse sex

parts.note: the eye is the organ of sight

indicators.note: something perverse is turned the wrong way round, so the word for sex is read backwards

parts.note: 'it' is old slang for sex, as in 'doing it'

explanation.surface: A crude Italian flashes his genitals before some kinky sex.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Organ' points at the obvious body part, but it is the eye. The answer is an offensive slang name for an Italian.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a derogatory slang term for a person from Italy, so it is literally a coarse word for one.

clue.text: Spear-carrier in unisex trainers

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the run of letters of the two words that follow

parts.note: the answer runs across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Someone carrying a spear while wearing gender-neutral running shoes.
explanation.definitionFit: A spear-carrier is a walk-on actor with no lines, the theatrical term for a minor background player.

clue.text: Pissed off — typical without an end to Blair

definitions.note: British slang for very drunk; an adjective like the answer

indicators.note: off means gone bad or wrong, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
a and an are both the indefinite article

indicators.note: the end of the name Blair, its final letter

parts.note: taken as written, its final letter used

explanation.surface: Someone fed up because the expected thing happened, minus any end to Tony Blair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pissed off' reads as angry, but the split is after 'Pissed', the British slang for drunk; 'off' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Paralytic is British slang for so drunk one cannot stand, a stronger word for being intoxicated.

clue.text: Brussels-style junkets for them?

definitions.meaning: Brussels is the seat of the European Parliament, so this points at Europe
junkets are trips at public expense, the perk a politician is famous for

explanation.walkthrough: The answer is EURO MPS, members of the European Parliament, who are mocked for jaunts paid for by taxpayers.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of the European Parliament sit in Brussels, and freebie trips are the stock satirical charge against them.

clue.text: Queen's rather common consort: unhealthy occupation

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a working-class casual partner of a gay man, queen being slang for one
second meaning: read literally, rough work that is bad for you

explanation.walkthrough: 'Queen' points at the monarch and her consort Prince Philip; here it is slang for a gay man.
explanation.definitionFit: Rough trade is slang for a casual sexual partner, often working-class, and the words also describe rough work.

clue.text: No ring about to be stuck in backside — endlessly happy

indicators.note: these letters are pushed inside the backside word
without its end, so its last letter goes

parts.note: butt is slang for the bottom

indicators.note: about means turned round, so these letters run backwards

parts.note: nay is an old word for no
O is ring-shaped

explanation.surface: A ring shoved up someone's backside, oddly leaving them cheerful.
explanation.definitionFit: Buoyant describes someone cheerful and in good spirits, floating along emotionally.

clue.text: Poor Nick, unshackled, without wife to give hand blow job

definitions.note: the work of a blow delivered by hand; a noun phrase like the answer

indicators.note: without means outside, so the anagram goes round the abbreviation for wife
poor means in bad shape, so these letters are reworked

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sex-work joke: a freed prisoner, wife absent, getting a hand job and a blow job.
explanation.walkthrough: A knuckle sandwich is slang for a punch in the mouth. The surface reads as sex acts; the definition is just a blow given with the hand.
explanation.definitionFit: A knuckle sandwich is jokey slang for a punch, a fist delivered to the face.

clue.text: Black Rod gets pole bust

definitions.note: a noun, the bosom; plural slang for breasts fits it

parts.note: Black Rod knocks on the door of the Commons at the State Opening of Parliament
S is the south pole

explanation.surface: A parliamentary official is arrested for dancing on a pole.
explanation.walkthrough: Black Rod is the British parliamentary official who bangs on the Commons door with his staff.
explanation.definitionFit: Knockers is slang for breasts, which together make up a woman's bust.

clue.text: Playing the ram? That's touching

definitions.meaning: first meaning: going a-butting, charging head first as a ram does
second meaning: next to, in contact

explanation.walkthrough: 'Playing the ram' suggests tupping; read as a-butting it is the ram's head-charging habit.
explanation.definitionFit: Abutting means bordering on or meeting at an edge, so two things abutting are in contact.

clue.text: Semi-stiff though shagged out

parts.note: semi- is the prefix for half
a stiff is slang for a corpse, so dead

explanation.surface: Only half aroused because he is worn out from sex.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shagged out' is British slang for exhausted.
explanation.definitionFit: Half-dead is a hyperbole for utterly worn out, which is what the British slang means.

clue.text: "Tabloid topless makes balls go curvy" releases

indicators.note: without its top, so the first letter goes; apt for the Sun's old topless models

parts.note: The Sun is Britain's best-known tabloid newspaper
in golf and cricket a hook sends the ball curving away

explanation.surface: A tabloid headline about a topless model making balls go curvy.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sun is a British tabloid famous for topless Page 3 photos, which the surface plays on.
explanation.definitionFit: To unhook something, such as a bra clasp, is to unfasten and let it go, a sense of setting free.

clue.text: Filthy hound's just in socks

indicators.note: dirty and messed up, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A dirty dog leaves muddy pawprints on someone wearing only socks.
explanation.definitionFit: Unshod means without shoes, so a person in only socks has bare footwear-free feet.

clue.text: Careless, gets sentimental about Labour's leader

indicators.note: about means around, so the word goes round the letter

parts.note: soppy means mawkishly sentimental

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter

parts.note: taken as written, its first letter used

explanation.surface: A slapdash politician going misty-eyed over the Labour leader.
explanation.definitionFit: Sloppy work is slapdash, done without care or attention.

clue.text: Run wild with nothing on and frig about, being common

indicators.note: running wild means out of control, so these letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: turned about, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: to frig and to lay are both crude slang for having sex

explanation.surface: Streaking and groping around, behaviour fit for a commoner.
explanation.definitionFit: Royalty sits above commoners, so someone common is literally not of royal blood.

clue.text: Blunder Fergie ultimately isn't able to take back

indicators.note: at the last, so the final letter of each word

parts.note: taken as written, its final letter used
taken as written, its final letter used; ultimately applies to both words
can't, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: The Duchess of York makes a gaffe she cannot retract.
explanation.walkthrough: Fergie is the nickname of Sarah, Duchess of York, a tabloid regular.
explanation.definitionFit: To recant is to withdraw a statement or belief formally, unsaying it.

clue.text: Spin: it's true, OK — open up a new career for yourself

definitions.text: open up a new career for yourself

indicators.note: spin means whirl round, so these letters are turned into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A spin doctor's line urging you to go off and try a new job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spin' looks like a noun for PR gloss, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To strike out is to set off independently on a fresh path, such as starting a different line of work.

clue.text: Nick the hack gets switched

parts.note: nick and can are both slang for prison
a hack is a journalist, and ED is the editor

explanation.surface: A journalist named Nick is moved to another job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nick' reads as a man's name; it is slang for prison.
explanation.definitionFit: A switch is a thin cane, so to be switched is to be beaten with one.

clue.text: The S — compared to The Sun? It's a grammatical thing

parts.note: set beside the full name, the short form has no u and n
the two missing letters at the end of the tabloid's name

explanation.surface: A media quiz: how does a paper called The S compare with The Sun?
explanation.walkthrough: Put 'The S' beside 'The Sun' and the difference is that it has NO UN. The Sun is a British tabloid.
explanation.definitionFit: A noun is a naming word, one of the parts of speech in grammar.

clue.text: More rum and yes-man loses head

indicators.note: the first letter is taken off

parts.note: a nodder agrees with everything, nodding along

explanation.surface: A sycophant drinking more rum until he passes out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rum' looks like the drink; it is the old British adjective for strange.
explanation.definitionFit: Rum is dated British slang for odd, so more rum is stranger.

clue.text: Dick squeezes point on Ms Lenska (not right — it sticks out a mile, maybe)

definitions.text: it sticks out a mile, maybe
definitions.note: a noun phrase describing a headland

indicators.note: the outer word holds the point tightly inside it

parts.note: dick is slang for the penis
N is a compass point

indicators.note: the letter for right is removed

parts.note: Rula Lenska is a British actress

explanation.surface: A smutty joke about an actress and an organ that 'sticks out a mile'.
explanation.walkthrough: Rula Lenska is a British TV actress. The surface wants the organ; the definition is a strip of land jutting into the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: A peninsula is land projecting into water, so it may well extend a mile or more from the coast.
